# Ghoṭamukha Sutta (MN 94 (PTS MN ii 157))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ghoṭamukha Sutta* (MN 94) is set at Benares in the Khemiya Mango Grove [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Along with the *Madhurasutta* (MN 84), it is distinguished within its division of the *Majjhimanikāya* by being set after the *parinibbāna* of the Buddha, opening with an interlocutor being informed that the Teacher has already attained final extinguishment [Norman 1983; von Hinüber 1996]. In the dialogue, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha approaches the venerable Udena and contends that there is no wanderers' or renunciate life that truly accords with the Dhamma [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral].
Udena gradually refutes Ghoṭamukha's skepticism and secures his conversion to the Buddhist path [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Dutt, Early History of the Spread of Buddhism; SuttaCentral]. During the discourse, the text distinguishes between two types of brahmins—those engrossed in worldly possessions, households, and wealth, and those who are unengrossed [Varma 1973]. It also features a passage concerning royal chaplains (*purohita*) and the ethical classification of four kinds of persons (such as those who torment themselves, torment others, or torment neither), a doctrinal exposition shared with the *Kandaraka Sutta* (MN 51) and the *Apaṇṇaka Sutta* (MN 60) [Bronkhorst 2011; DharmaNexus]. In an appendix to the sutta, Ghoṭamukha finances the construction of a communal assembly hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*), known as the Ghoṭamukhī hall, for the Sangha at Pāṭaliputta [Humphreys 1956; Dutt, Early History of the Spread of Buddhism; von Hinüber 1996].
A Sanskrit fragment from the Turfan finds (SHT sutta 64) is identified as a parallel to this discourse and its counterpart in MN 51 [Waldschmidt 1971; SuttaCentral]. The text shares extensive textual reuse across the Pali Canon, most notably with the *Kandaraka Sutta* (MN 51), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4.198), the *Catukkapuggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.4), the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10.99), and the *Devadaha Sutta* (MN 101) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns several doctrinal segments with Chinese Āgama collections (including the *Madhyama Āgama*, T 26) as well as Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and *Prajñāpāramitā* texts [DharmaNexus].
